John Foxe
FOKS
proper noun
From the English surname Foxe; the author of the Acts and Monuments, known as Foxe’s Book of Martyrs.

Biblical Definition

John Foxe was an English Protestant of the sixteenth century, the author of the great work Acts and Monuments, known to all later ages as Foxe’s Book of Martyrs. In it he gathered the histories of the witnesses who had suffered for the gospel, from the early church through the long centuries to the Marian fires of his own day, when Cranmer, Latimer, Ridley, and hundreds more were burned for the Reformed faith under Queen Mary. The book became, after the Bible, the most cherished volume in English Protestant homes, and it shaped the conscience of a nation. The dictionary honours Foxe for preserving the memory of the martyrs, who overcame the accuser by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony, and loved not their lives unto the death (Rev 12:11), and whose souls John saw under the altar, slain for the word of God and the testimony which they held (Rev 6:9). They were of those who were tortured, not accepting deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection (Heb 11:35). Where critics have shown that Foxe sometimes gathered his tales uncritically, the substance of his record stands; and his book remains a monument to the truth that blessed are the dead which die in the Lord (Rev 14:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

The sixteenth-century author of the Acts and Monuments, Foxe’s Book of Martyrs, who preserved the memory of the Protestant martyrs.

JOHN FOXE, the sixteenth-century author of the Acts and Monuments.

His book is known to all ages as Foxe’s Book of Martyrs.

It gathered the histories of those who suffered for the gospel.

It records the Marian martyrs Cranmer, Latimer, Ridley, and many more.

After the Bible it was the most cherished book in English Protestant homes.

Key Scripture

Rev 6:9 — "And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:"

Rev 12:11 — "And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death."

Heb 11:35 — "Women received their dead raised to life again: and others were tortured, not accepting deliverance; that they might obtain a better resurrection:"

Rev 14:13 — "And I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them."

Modern Corruption

His book preserved the memory of the martyrs burned by Rome, shaping the conscience of Protestant England.

expand to see more

The corruption Foxe’s book lays bare is the persecuting fury of Rome, which answered the Reformed gospel with prison, rack, and fire. He set down the histories of the martyrs that their witness might not be forgotten, and that England might know at what price the gospel had been kept. The dictionary honours this labour of memory, which preserved for the church the testimony of those who loved not their lives unto the death.

What is honourable in Foxe is the substance of his record and the devotion it kindled. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the honouring of the martyrs and the cost of the truth. Where Foxe at times gathered his accounts uncritically, as later study has shown, the great body of his record stands, and the verdict of heaven over his martyrs stands sure: blessed are the dead which die in the Lord, who rest from their labours while their works follow them. A people that forgets its martyrs will not long keep their faith.
